sources.entry: Shipping to Production, The Pragmatic Programmer

summary.title: Shipping to Production
summary.one_liner: You learn the spectrum of production release practices, from YOLO shipping to multi-stage verification, and the principles, tools and pragmatic risk-taking that make releases fast and reliable.
takeaways: Shipping sits on a spectrum from YOLO changes made directly in production to heavyweight multi-stage verification, and the right point depends on how many customers depend on the product.

Typical release processes differ by company type: startups skip many checks, traditional companies rely on QA and scheduled releases, and large tech companies invest in automation, canarying and feature flags.
Core principles include local verification, edge-case testing, automated tests in CI, code review, monitoring key metrics, and an on-call rotation with runbooks.
Additional safety nets include separate environments, spinning up environments dynamically, exploratory testing, canarying, feature flags, staged rollouts, multi-tenancy and automated rollbacks.
Pragmatic risk-taking means deciding which steps are never bypassed, notifying stakeholders about risky changes, and having an easy rollback plan.
summary.summary: The article, by Gergely Orosz of The Pragmatic Engineer, surveys how teams ship code to production reliably and quickly. It contrasts YOLO shipping with thorough multi-stage verification, then describes typical release processes at startups, traditional companies, large tech companies and Facebook. It goes on to list responsible shipping principles, additional safety-net approaches such as canarying, feature flags, staged rollouts and automated rollbacks, and pragmatic ways to take risks to move faster. Examples draw on Uber, Booking.com, Facebook and other companies, with links to further reading.
